citation: Haj-Bolouri, A. (2023). The experience of immersive virtual reality: A phenomenology inspired inquiry. Communications of the Association for Information Systems, 52, Article 38, 782-814. https://doi.org/10.17705/1CAIS.05238
thesis: Existing IS research on Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) has not clarified how the IVR experience becomes meaningful for end-users. Undertaking a phenomenological inquiry based on Heidegger's (1962) Being and Time -- specifically his notions of meaning, meaningfulness, and world -- and operationalized through phenomenological interviewing and Interpretive Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) within an empirical case of IVR fire-safety training at SJ (Sweden's largest train operator), the study unveils four characteristics of the IVR experience as a 'meaningful escapism': Sense of Content, Sense of Familiarity, Sense of Mood, and Sense of Care. On this basis the paper proposes 'Virtual Dasein' (being-in-the-virtual-world) as an extension of Heidegger's Dasein (being-in-the-world) for IS theorizing about IVR. The inquiry engages Heidegger's general mood/meaning/care apparatus from Being and Time throughout; it does not engage his boredom analysis (Langeweile) or Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics at all.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.summary: States the IS research gap on meaningful IVR experience, previews the four characteristics and 'Virtual Dasein.'

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Technology-and-the-real framing (Vattimo, Bostrom's simulation argument, Plato's Cave); IVR market growth and Metaverse context; IS precedent (Walsh & Pawlowski 2002, 'a technology in need for IS research'); states RQ1 (how individuals use the IVR experience to create meaning in the context of meaningful escapism) and four reasons the study matters to the IS field.

sections.title: 2.1 What is Reality?
sections.summary: Surveys realism, idealism, phenomenalism, representationalism, and critical realism (Bhaskar); Kant's Ding-an-sich; argues for a middle way compatible with the socio-technical view in IS, oriented toward being-in-the-world (Dreyfus).

sections.title: 2.2 What is Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR)?
sections.summary: Traces 'virtual' from scholastic philosophy through early computer-simulation definitions (Heim 2000; Steuer 1995) to HMD-based IVR; discusses Penny's (1993) critique of virtual reality as reinforcing Cartesian dualism via a 'virtual body' image.

sections.title: 2.3 What Signifies the Immersive Virtual Reality Experience?
sections.summary: Distinguishes physical from psychological immersion; defines presence via Biocca & Levy (2013) as feeling present in the mediated rather than physical environment when attention is fully directed to the IVR environment; discusses IVR's freedom from ordinary cause-and-effect (teleportation, no injury from falling).

sections.title: 2.4 Why is the Immersive Virtual Reality Experience an Escapism?
sections.summary: Contrasts Evans's (2001) negative view of escapism (avoidance, denial, addiction) with Hazzard's (2016) positive view (broadening the world, exploring safely); previews the study's dual-sword framing of escapism.

sections.title: 3.1 Heidegger's Phenomenological View on World, Meaning, and Meaningfulness
sections.summary: Names Husserl (consciousness), Merleau-Ponty (bodily perception), and Heidegger (Dasein/being-in-the-world) as the three streams of phenomenology, commits explicitly to the Heideggerian one; Table 1 catalogs prior Heideggerian IS scholarship (Dourish, Ehn, Harnesk & Thapa, Introna, Mingers, Osmundsen et al., Monod et al., Riemer & Johnston, Waller & Johnston, Winograd & Flores); Table 2 formalizes the meaning (representational/created/attributed) vs. meaningfulness (subjective/experienced/significant) distinction; notes Heidegger's own theme was 'to transcend' the world, not 'to escape' it.

sections.title: 3.2 Operationalizing the Phenomenology Inspired Inquiry
sections.summary: 3.2.1 sets the empirical horizon: SJ fire-safety training in IVR since late 2020, a five-step training scenario (equip HMD/fire-hose replica -> instructor briefing -> teleport into scenario -> trial-and-error fire extinguishing -> debrief dialogue). 3.2.2 details data collection (Bevan 2014 phenomenological-interview structure, Table 3: descriptive-hermeneutic attitude, reflexive dialogue, active listening) and analysis (Eatough & Smith 2017 IPA in NVivo 12, Table 4: 812 open codes -> 17 initial themes -> 4 axially-coded characteristics; memo-writing reported as '50 memos' in prose but '46 memos' in Table 4, an internal inconsistency).

sections.title: 4. Characteristics of the IVR Experience as a Meaningful Escapism
sections.summary: 4.1 Sense of Content (Flow through World/creating meaning) -- interviewees value freedom from real-world consequence and constraint. 4.2 Sense of Familiarity (Orientation to/from World/recognizing meaning) -- prior real-train knowledge aids navigation; teleportation causes disorientation/dizziness for some. 4.3 Sense of Mood (Imagining/Perceiving a World/enacting meaning) -- a glitching fire-hose replica shifts training mood from serious to funny. 4.4 Sense of Care (Agency/Becoming Possibilities in World/actualizing meaning) -- meaningfulness contingent on transferability of virtual-world skills to real-world practice. Twelve SJ participants (train operators, train drivers, one instructor) are quoted throughout.

sections.title: 5.1 A Nuanced Perspective of the IVR Experience as a Meaningful Escapism
sections.summary: Distinguishes an IVR experience 'filled with meaning' from one that 'feels meaningful'; discusses how mood carried into/from IVR (loneliness, angst, thrill) affects care; introduces 'breakdown situations' (obstinate vs. obstructive, borrowed from Dreyfus 1991/2002 -- explicitly not Heidegger's own term) via the fire-hose glitch example.

sections.title: 5.2 Implications of Phenomenology for IVR Research in the IS Field
sections.summary: Proposes 'Virtual Dasein' (being-in-the-virtual-world) as an alternative/extension of Dasein; discusses 'co-extensive spaces' (Saker & Frith 2020) and poses future research questions about what is escaped (body/senses/mood) when one becomes Virtual Dasein.

sections.title: 5.3 Contributions to the IS Field and Implications for IS Research
sections.summary: States design-science contributions (justificatory/kernel knowledge for design principles, per Gregor & Jones 2007; Gregor & Hevner 2013); the meaning/meaningfulness conceptual clarification; ethical concerns about escapism's potential for addiction and societal withdrawal, referencing Facebook's Metaverse.

sections.title: 6. Conclusion
sections.summary: Restates the two headline claims (physical-world Dasein concerned with mattering to the lifeworld; virtual-world 'Virtual Dasein' as an extension); names limitations (Heidegger's complexity simplified for an IS audience; single empirical context of fire-safety training).

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: central to Sense of Content ('Flow through World'); interviewees describe frictionless, constraint-free engagement once physical-world representational limits (walls, furniture, injury) are lifted; no Csikszentmihalyi-style flow-state theory cited

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: meaninglessness (not monotony) operative as meaningfulness's contrast term throughout; an experience can be 'filled with meaning' without becoming meaningful, and a virtual-world skill can become 'meaningless' if not actualizable in the physical world; monotony/repetitive-stimulus design not discussed

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: treated only in the engaged/absorbed direction, the inverse of the controlled vocabulary's disengagement framing: presence defined as attention 'fully directed towards the IVR environment and not the physical space'

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: near-miss, not a match: documents temporal compression ('forgetting about time') under psychological immersion, and a 'historicity and temporality of meaning' bound up with Sense of Care -- a temporality of mattering, not felt time-dilation

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form)

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.signal: qualitative-interview modality, not a psychometric scale -- structured phenomenological interviewing per Bevan's (2014) three-stage framework (descriptive-narrative context questions -> descriptive/structural 'modes of appearing' questions -> imaginative-variation questions)
measures.apparatus: semi-structured interview protocol (Table 3) plus researcher observation of training sessions; Eatough & Smith's (2017) Interpretive Phenomenological Analysis (open coding -> focused coding -> axial coding -> memo-writing) conducted in NVivo 12
measures.sampleN: 12 participants (train conductors/operators, train drivers, and one instructor) from SJ, Sweden's largest train operator
measures.keyResult: 812 line-by-line open codes reduced to 17 focused/initial themes, axially coded into 4 characteristics of the IVR experience as meaningful escapism (Sense of Content, Sense of Familiarity, Sense of Mood, Sense of Care); memo-writing reported inconsistently within the source itself as '50 memos' in prose (p.794) vs. '46 memos' in the summary table (Table 4, same page)

measures.label: EEG frontal alpha asymmetry
measures.note: not present; no physiological instrumentation anywhere in the source

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.note: not present; training performance is discussed narratively (trial-and-error extinguishing) but never quantified as RT/error data

readings.claim: Four characteristics of meaningfulness -- Sense of Content, Sense of Familiarity, Sense of Mood, Sense of Care -- each paired with a feature of escapism (Flow through World, Orientation to/from World, Imagining/Perceiving a World, Agency/Becoming Possibilities in World respectively) -- answer RQ1.

Meaning (representational, created, attributed -- intelligibility) is conceptually distinct from meaningfulness (subjective, experienced, significant -- mattering to the lifeworld via mood and care); an experience can be 'filled with meaning' without becoming meaningful.
Escapism is a 'dual sword': it supplies safety, freedom from real-world consequence, and low-risk rehearsal, but also disorientation and a risk of addiction/withdrawal if pursued to excess.
readings.stance: qualifies (synthesizes negative and positive prior views)

readings.claim: 'Breakdown situations' (obstinate = temporary malfunction; obstructive = permanent failure), a distinction borrowed from Dreyfus's reading of Heidegger rather than Heidegger's own vocabulary, differentiate malfunctions that stimulate Sense of Care from those that collapse the IVR experience into a merely present-at-hand object.
readings.stance: extends (via secondary literature, explicitly flagged as non-Heideggerian terminology)

readings.claim: 'Virtual Dasein' (being-in-the-virtual-world) is proposed as an extension of Heidegger's Dasein (being-in-the-world) for theorizing IVR in IS.

The study demonstrates the viability of phenomenology, specifically Heideggerian phenomenology, for IVR research in the IS field, extending an existing lineage of Heideggerian IS scholarship (Table 1) not previously applied to IVR.

Findings are limited by the simplification of Heidegger's complex phenomenology for an IS (not philosophical) audience, and by confinement to a single empirical context (IVR fire-safety training); generalization to other IVR domains is left to future research.

concepts.gloss: being-in-the-virtual-world; the paper's proposed extension of Heidegger's Dasein for IVR
meaning = representational/created/attributed intelligibility; meaningfulness = subjective significance mattering to the lifeworld via mood and care
the paper's framing of the IVR experience: a fleeting feeling of escape that becomes meaningful through Content, Familiarity, Mood, and Care

concepts.term: Sense of Content / Sense of Familiarity / Sense of Mood / Sense of Care
concepts.gloss: the four characteristics unveiled via IPA, each paired with a 'feature of escapism'
Dreyfus's (1991, 2002) distinction between temporary and permanent disruptions of ready-to-hand practice, applied here to IVR malfunction
feeling present in the mediated (virtual) rather than physical environment, per Biocca & Levy (2013)
Saker & Frith's (2020) term for the simultaneous physical/virtual situatedness of mobile IVR, cited to complicate a strict extend-vs-escape dualism
Eatough & Smith's (2017) qualitative analysis method: open coding -> focused coding -> axial coding -> memo-writing
three-stage interview structure: descriptive-narrative context questions, descriptive/structural questions of modes of appearing, imaginative-variation questions

tensions.axis: phenomenological/lived-experience approach to IVR (this paper) vs. representationalism / Cartesian-dualist ontology of presence (dominant in Computer Science and HCI: Biocca, Durlach & Slater, Heeter, Held & Durlach, Lombard & Ditton, Loomis)
tensions.note: the paper positions its Heideggerian approach as going 'beyond the ontological assumptions of representationalism,' explicitly contesting the field's default presence-theory ontology while still designing its own empirical case (SJ fire-safety training) on representational premises

the paper synthesizes both into a 'dual sword' framing rather than adjudicating between them, but leans toward the positive/meaningful reading for its own empirical case while retaining an ethical caution about excess

tensions.axis: general Being-and-Time mood/attunement doctrine (this paper's actual framework) vs. FCM's boredom-specific mood typology (not engaged)
tensions.note: the paper cites Heidegger's claim that Dasein is always in some mood, including indifference, but never specializes this into a boredom analysis; a genuine but unexploited proximity to this cluster's core FCM material
